ingredients.item: Kosher salt (5% of the salmon's weight)

instructions: Two days ahead: cut the salmon into 4 fillets about 1 inch thick. Pour the 2 tbsp sake over them, turn them so both sides are coated, and leave them for 10 minutes.

Weigh the salmon. The salt is 5% of its weight, so for 1 1/2 lbs that's 34 g, about 3 1/2 tbsp of Diamond Crystal kosher salt. Pat the fillets dry with paper towels, sprinkle some of the salt over the skin, then the rest over both sides.
Line an airtight container with paper towels. Lay the fillets in it skin side up with paper towels between them and on top. Cover and refrigerate for 2 days.

Rinse the rice in cold water until it runs mostly clear. Put it in a medium pot with 1 3/4 cups water, bring it to a boil over high heat, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes. Leave it covered off the heat for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile, set a rack about 9 inches from the broiler and heat the broiler to high for 5 minutes. Line a baking sheet with foil and rub the 1 tsp oil over it.
Peel the 3-inch piece of daikon and grate it. Squeeze it gently so it stays moist but isn't dripping.
Take the fillets out of the container and throw away the wet paper towels. Pat the fillets dry and lay them skin side up on the baking sheet.
Broil the salmon for 8 to 10 minutes without flipping, until the skin is browned and the flesh flakes when you press the thickest part with a fork.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Serve the salmon with the rice and the grated daikon.
advance_prep_notes: salt the salmon 2 days ahead and refrigerate it
method_notes: Cup of Yum and Just One Cookbook give the same method: sake on the fillets, salt at 5% of the weight, a 2 day cure between paper towels in the fridge, then broil skin side up for 8 to 10 minutes and serve with grated daikon. Food Republic salts for only 2 to 5 hours and finishes the skin over the grill, and The Daily Meal rinses off the salt after 1 hour. This one follows Cup of Yum for the cure and the broiling. Short-grain rice comes from Food Republic's rice serving. The cure is the dish, so it is written as the first step; the faster ones give a less seasoned fillet.
